why:
Both forces act along the same straight line, so they add algebraically once each is given a sign. Taking \(+x\) as positive, the 10 N force contributes \(+10\) N and the 15 N force contributes \(-15\) N:
\(F_{\text{net}} = (+10) + (-15) = -5\) N
The negative sign means the resultant points along the \(-x\)-axis, so it is a 5 N force along the \(-x\)-axis.

Why the others fail: the two 25 N alternatives come from ADDING the magnitudes, which is only valid for parallel forces pointing the same way. These two are anti-parallel, so their magnitudes SUBTRACT - the chapter states this for anti-parallel vectors as \(|\overrightarrow{AC}| = ||\overrightarrow{AB}| - |\overrightarrow{BC}||\). The remaining alternative has the right magnitude but the wrong sense: the resultant of two anti-parallel forces always points along the LARGER of the two, and the larger force here (15 N) acts along \(-x\).

A vector is specified by a magnitude AND a direction, so two vectors can only be equal when BOTH agree. The chapter defines it in exactly those terms: two vectors representing the same physical quantity are equal if and only if they have the same magnitude and direction.

Why the others fail: equal magnitude alone leaves the direction free, so \(3\hat{i}\) and \(3\hat{j}\) would count as equal though they point along different axes. Equal direction alone leaves the length free, so \(\hat{i}\) and \(5\hat{i}\) would count as equal. Same magnitude with OPPOSITE direction is the definition of a negative vector \(\left(\vec{B} = -\vec{A}\right)\), which is the exact opposite of equality.

The scalar product is \(\vec{P} \cdot \vec{Q} = PQ\cos\theta\). For two unit vectors \(P = Q = 1\), and perpendicular means \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\):
\(\vec{P} \cdot \vec{Q} = (1)(1)\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\)
So the magnitude of the scalar product is zero. This is the result the chapter uses to write \(\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{k} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{i} = 0\).

Why the others fail: a value of 1 requires \(\cos\theta = 1\), i.e. parallel unit vectors \(\left(\theta = 0\right)\); a value of \(-1\) requires \(\cos\theta = -1\), i.e. anti-parallel unit vectors \(\left(\theta = 180^{\circ}\right)\); and 2 is impossible, since \(|\cos\theta| \le 1\) caps the scalar product of two unit vectors at 1.

The magnitude of the vector product is \(|\vec{P} \times \vec{Q}| = PQ\sin\theta\). For two unit vectors \(P = Q = 1\), and \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\):
\(|\vec{P} \times \vec{Q}| = (1)(1)\sin 60^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866\)

Why the others fail: a value of 1 needs \(\sin\theta = 1\), i.e. \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\), not \(60^{\circ}\). Both 2 and \(3/2\) exceed 1, and since \(\sin\theta \le 1\) the vector product of two UNIT vectors can never have a magnitude greater than 1 - so those two are impossible for any angle whatever, not merely wrong for this one.

Take the four statements in turn.

The two statements about the SCALAR product are both true. The scalar product is distributive over addition, \(\vec{A} \cdot \left(\vec{B} + \vec{C}\right) = \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} + \vec{A} \cdot \vec{C}\), and it is commutative, \(\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}\), because \(PQ\cos\theta = QP\cos\theta\). The chapter lists both among the characteristics of the scalar product.

The statement \(\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}\) is NOT correct, and that is what the question is asking for. The vector product does not obey the commutative law: by the right-hand screw rule, turning from \(\vec{A}\) to \(\vec{B}\) advances the screw one way and turning from \(\vec{B}\) to \(\vec{A}\) advances it the opposite way, so the two products have equal magnitudes and OPPOSITE directions:
\(\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -\left(\vec{B} \times \vec{A}\right)\)
The chapter states this as the first characteristic of the vector product, \(\vec{P} \times \vec{Q} \ne \vec{Q} \times \vec{P}\), adding that \(|\vec{P} \times \vec{Q}| = |\vec{Q} \times \vec{P}|\) but their directions are opposite. The two sides are therefore equal only in the degenerate case where both products vanish (parallel or anti-parallel vectors), never in general.

Note on the printed question: the fourth statement is ALSO not correct as it appears in the textbook. It is printed \(\vec{A} \times \left(\vec{B} + \vec{C}\right) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{B} \times \vec{C}\), whose second term should read \(\vec{A} \times \vec{C}\) - the textbook itself prints the distributive law for the vector product correctly elsewhere in this chapter as \(\vec{A} \times \left(\vec{B} + \vec{C}\right) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{A} \times \vec{C}\). So the question as printed has two statements that are not correct rather than one. The key is kept on the anti-commutativity statement, which is false as a matter of physics rather than through a misprint; if you picked the distributive statement on the strength of its printed second term, you were reading the page correctly.
